content: Tarpons are large fish belonging to the genus Megalops. There are two species of tarpons: Megalops atlanticus (Atlantic tarpon) and Megalops cyprinoides (Indo-Pacific tarpon). These are the only members of the family Megalopidae. The Atlantic tarpon is distributed along the western Atlantic coast from Virginia to Brazil, including the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean, as well as the eastern Atlantic coast from Senegal to South Angola. The Indo-Pacific tarpon is found along the eastern African coast, throughout Southeast Asia, Japan, Tahiti, and Australia. Both species inhabit both saltwater and freshwater environments, often traveling upriver to access freshwater marshes. They are capable of surviving in brackish water, environments with varying pH levels, and areas with low dissolved oxygen due to their specialized swim bladders, which function as respiratory organs. Tarpons can also surface to gulp air, which provides them with a temporary energy boost. The habitats of tarpons vary depending on their developmental stage. Stage-one larvae are typically found in warm, clear oceanic waters near the surface. Stage-two and stage-three larvae inhabit salt marshes, tidal pools, creeks, and rivers, which are generally warm, shallow, and dark with sandy or muddy bottoms. Juvenile tarpons often ascend rivers into freshwater habitats. As they mature into adults, they return to the open ocean, although some remain in freshwater environments. Tarpons can grow to lengths of 4 to 8 feet and weigh between 60 and 280 pounds. They have soft dorsal and anal rays, bluish or greenish backs, and distinctive lateral lines. Their bodies are covered in shiny, silvery scales, except for their heads. They have large eyes with adipose eyelids and broad mouths with prominent lower jaws that extend beyond the rest of the face. Tarpons are known for their acrobatic behavior, particularly when hooked. They often leap out of the water multiple times, making them challenging to catch. These jumps can also occur unexpectedly, posing a risk to anglers even before the fish is hooked. Tarpons reproduce offshore in warm, isolated areas. Females are highly fecund, capable of laying up to 12 million eggs in a single spawning event. Sexual maturity is reached when they grow to a length of 75 to 125 cm. Spawning typically occurs from late spring to early summer. Their life cycle consists of three distinct developmental stages, each associated with different habitats. The first stage, known as the leptocephalus stage, lasts 20 to 30 days and occurs in warm, clear oceanic waters near the surface. During this stage, the larvae shrink in size as they transition to stage two, a process characterized by a period of negative growth followed by slow growth. By day 70, the fish enter the juvenile growth phase (stage three), during which they grow rapidly until reaching sexual maturity. The diet of tarpons changes as they develop. Stage-one larvae do not actively forage but instead absorb nutrients from seawater through their skin. Stage-two and stage-three juveniles primarily consume zooplankton, along with insects and small fish. As they grow, particularly in freshwater environments, their diet expands to include insects, fish, crabs, and grass shrimp. Adult tarpons are strictly carnivorous, feeding on midwater prey, which they swallow whole. They are nocturnal hunters. Predation on tarpons varies by life stage. During stage one and early stage two, their primary predators are other fish, depending on the size of the tarpon. Juveniles are preyed upon by larger juvenile tarpons and piscivorous birds. They are particularly vulnerable to birds when surfacing for air, as their rolling motion and silvery scales make them conspicuous. Adult tarpons occasionally fall prey to sharks, porpoises, crocodiles, and alligators. A unique feature of tarpons is their swim bladder, which functions as a respiratory pseudo-organ. This unpaired structure, located dorsally from the posterior pharynx, is lined with blood capillaries and a thin epithelium, resembling alveolar tissue. This adaptation allows tarpons to breathe air at the surface, a behavior mediated by visual cues. The frequency of their air-breathing is inversely related to the dissolved oxygen content of the water. Tarpons are obligate air breathers, meaning they must surface to breathe; otherwise, they will die. The rolling motion they use to breathe is a characteristic behavior often associated with tarpon sightings. Tarpons are highly prized as saltwater game fish due to their size, strength, and acrobatic leaping ability. However, their meat is not considered desirable, so most tarpons are released after being caught. Numerous fishing tournaments are dedicated to catching tarpons. The geographical distribution and migration patterns of tarpons are not well-documented, as they are not commercially valuable as food fish. They inhabit both sides of the Atlantic Ocean, with their eastern Atlantic range extending from Senegal to the Congo. In the western Atlantic, they are primarily found in warmer coastal waters, including the Gulf of Mexico, Florida, and the West Indies. However, they are also caught as far north as Cape Hatteras and Nova Scotia and as far south as Bermuda and Argentina. Scientific studies have shown that tarpons have migrated through the Panama Canal between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans for over 70 years, although they are not known to breed in the Pacific. Anecdotal evidence from fishing guides and anglers supports this, with reports of juvenile and adult tarpons being caught on the Pacific side of Panama, including locations such as the Bayano River, the Gulf of San Miguel, Coiba Island, and Piñas Bay. Tarpons tolerate a wide range of salinities and are opportunistic feeders, which allows them to migrate extensively. However, their movements are limited by water temperature. Tarpons prefer temperatures between 72 and 82°F (22 to 28°C) and become inactive below 60°F (15.6°C). Temperatures below 40°F (4.5°C) can be lethal.
